items.title: WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?
items.summary:
Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw

Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The manager said the centre-back, who had not asked to come off and walked straight down the tunnel, had taken a knock to the head in training and been assessed and cleared, but that during the game “she was not herself”. On came Veerle Buurman and the threat of Khadija Shaw was nullified, the Dutch defender restricting the golden boot favourite so well that Shaw did not manage a shot on target. Bompastor said after the game that she had not spoken to Buchanan but that she would “explain myself to her”. “I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I’m always direct and honest so they have the information,” she said. “It won’t be any different.” Enforced or not, the substitution was a huge gamble that paid off, even after the loss of Melvine Malard to injury in the first half reduced their number of remaining in-game substitution windows to one. Suzanne Wrack

Match report: Chelsea 1-0 Manchester City
items.t: WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?

Jay Shah has been re-elected unopposed as chair of the International Cricket Council after a board meeting in Bali that has also paved the way for the expansion of the Indian Premier League. In announcing their major events schedule until 2035, the ICC has moved all of their global tournaments to the second half of the year, creating a three-month period, from March to May, that is expected to be filled by the IPL.

In the past two years, the men’s T20 World Cup and Champions Trophy have been played in February and March. The Future Tours Programme governing bilateral series between ICC members has yet to be signed off, but sources involved in those discussions have indicated that no major series will be scheduled during those months.

The San Francisco 49ers quarterback was long seen as the beneficiary of the tools at his disposal. This season, he’s setting fire to that narrative

Purdy has presided over lots of routs since he took over the offense in 2022, but this particular defeat of the Cowboys had a unique feel to it.

Purdy, who is often dismissed as benefiting from a hospitable 49ers system, was a wrecking crew. That was true in the statistical sense, as Purdy closed with 389 yards and three touchdowns on 22-of-28 passing. Later in the game, it became true in the literal sense as Purdy ended one of his greatest games in style.

items.title: Wales’ epic upset against All Blacks offers fresh hope for rank outsiders | Robert Kitson
items.summary:
The plot twist in Cardiff that nobody saw coming suggests the northern hemisphere is remobilising in time for next year’s World Cup

What does it take to beat the All Blacks in Cardiff? “I’ll never forget the pressure they put us under. I don’t think we were a better team than New Zealand, but there was a certain spirit in the Welsh side which pulled us through.” The vivid recollections of the late, great Cliff Morgan on Wales’s famous victory in 1953 could just as easily have applied to the long-awaited modern-day sequel on Saturday.

Seventy-three years. The last time it came to pass was the year Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay officially became the first people to conquer Everest. Some bookmakers had even stopped taking bets on an All Blacks win; in the buildup the Wales side were likened in one New Zealand newspaper to “Dickensian orphans” begging for scraps. More bread of heaven, please sir? Here was a plot twist nobody saw coming.

items.title: European football body’s plan to go global leaves Fifa on tenterhooks
items.summary:
Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome

It will be one of the most eagerly anticipated documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed. In September the increasingly powerful European Football Clubs body announced a “feasibility study” into exactly how it can become established on a more global scale, morphing into an organisation that represents clubs all over the world.

The study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future. It has the potential to transform a landscape destabilised by the scandals surrounding Fifa and Gianni Infantino. Once considered a lobby group representing clubs’ interests in the face of domineering governing bodies, EFC has mushroomed into a behemoth with almost 1,000 members that has the potential to supplant them.

items.title: Three Lions’ win over Spain comes in two acts: the first superb, the second heroic | Sid Lowe
items.summary:
Visitors take game to world champions and, though their hold on possession plummets, their rearguard is outstanding

In the final, absurdly tense moments before England finally did it and Spain finally fell, when Dan Burn had been sent on to do Dan Burn things, when the board had gone up with a 4 on but the clock wasn’t moving fast enough and the men in red kept coming back, Harry Kane had come to the side of the pitch to stand beside Thomas Tuchel. Palms out, Kane signalled and directed and appealed with his teammates to hold on to what they had: somehow, anyhow. What they had was special, but their grip on it was not as secure as it had seemed. Not as secure as it should have been too.

Tuchel gave Kane a nudge that looked pretty playful considering the pressure, before Marc Bollengier, the fourth official, ordered him back to the bench. But England’s captain was not gone for long and when he returned he was joined by almost all of them, awaiting the big moment. From there, he watched James Trafford make an astonishing double save, a moment of heroism that allowed them to hang on. Then, standing alongside the rest who could no longer just sit there, he saw the last header clear – Dan Burn things – before the whistle went. Then he and they went on one last run, back on to the pitch.

Continue reading...
items.t: Three Lions’ win over Spain comes in two acts: the first superb, the second heroic | Sid Lowe

items.title: Mirra Andreeva holds nerve against Svitolina to win WTA Finals for first time
items.summary:
• Andreeva seals 7-5, 6-3 victory to earn world No 2 ranking

  • Russian dominates tournament without losing a set

Mirra Andreeva had put herself on the brink of securing another effortless, straightforward set in one of the biggest finals of her career when she momentarily balked. Serving for the first set at 5-4, Andreeva nervously opened the game with two dire double faults before spraying two further unforced errors to hand over the break.

There have already been many times in Andreeva’s young career when similar sequences triggered epic, dramatic collapses, so prone the 19-year-old has been to losing her composure when things do not go her way. This time, she betrayed no negative emotions at all. Andreeva immediately retrieved the break and regained her momentum as she marched to a monumental victory, defeating Elina Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 to win the WTA Finals at Indian Wells for the first time.

items.summary:
Reece Walsh got the better of Kalyn Ponga in the battle of the fullbacks as Australia won a fourth-straight title by doing the small things better

In sport and life, the difference between winning and losing is often in small margins. A sliver of sandpaper has had Australian cricket tearing itself to pieces all week. An entire AFL season came down to a fan bell that ignited four goals in five minutes. A single point decided the NRL title. A high tackle send-off swung the Origin series. Often, a fraction too much friction is all that separates greatness from madness.

Australia and New Zealand were contesting their first World Cup final since 2013. In those 13 years, the gap between nations had closed. On Sunday night in Brisbane it started dead level.

items.title: Emotional Rory McIlroy dedicates record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title to father
items.summary:
• McIlroy’s father, Gerry, is recovering after major surgery

  • ‘He said: “Go and win the Race to Dubai.” This is for him’

An emotional Rory McIlroy dedicated a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title to his father, Gerry, who is recovering from major surgery in the United States. McIlroy was reduced to tears when recalling the parting message from McIlroy Sr as he headed for the closing events in the DP World Tour’s season.

McIlroy’s final round of 67 at the DP World Tour Championship in Dubai helped him to finish in second place, which was sufficient to edge out Eugenio Chacarra for the season-long order of merit crown. Tyrrell Hatton won the tournament itself, with Chacarra’s share of third meaning McIlroy prevailed by the narrow margin of 125 points. He later revealed Gerry had been at the forefront of his mind.

items.title: History, euphoria and no more dreaming – are Wales back after win over All Blacks?
items.summary:
Seismic victory in Cardiff was cathartic and though Steve Tandy urges caution, maybe the ‘Welsh problem’ can be fixed

So that’s that fixed then. Wales are back and all is right with the world. Suddenly the dysfunction at the union, the financial plight, the disputes, the emptying stadiums, the defeats – oh, the defeats – feel a very long way away. The All Blacks have been beaten. Seventy-three years of hurt, no more need for dreaming.

The euphoria in the Principality Stadium, however many people were there – or more pertinently not – seemed as eerily familiar as it was cathartic. This was how Cardiff used to feel on match day.
